target_audience: University students with a basic interest in computer science and cryptography

sections.title: Introduction: Cryptographic Hash Functions
sections.content: Define hashing as a digital fingerprint. Explain the concept of a 'one-way function'—easy to compute in one direction, impossible to reverse.
sections.example: Imagine a 'Magic Blender': You can put a whole fruit salad in and get a unique 64-character smoothie recipe, but you can never turn the smoothie back into the original fruit.

sections.title: The Proof-of-Work Math: Solving the Puzzle
sections.content: Introduce the SHA-256 algorithm. Explain that Bitcoin requires finding a specific 'nonce' (a random number) that, when combined with transaction data, produces a hash starting with a specific number of zeros.
sections.example: A digital treasure hunt: Miners are like monkeys at typewriters trying to find the one password that opens a digital lock, where the difficulty is adjusted to ensure it takes 10 minutes.

sections.title: Public-Key Cryptography: Who Owns the Coins?
sections.content: Explain Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC). Introduce the relationship between a Private Key (a secret number) and a Public Key (a point on an elliptic curve derived from the private key).
sections.example: Use a 'Lock and Key' analogy: Your Private Key is the secret key to open the vault, and your Public Key is the transparent glass address box where people can safely deposit gold bars.

sections.title: Digital Signatures: Proving Ownership
sections.content: Demonstrate how the Private Key acts as a mathematical 'seal' on a transaction. The network uses the Public Key to verify the signature without ever seeing the Private Key.
sections.example: A magical wax seal: You use your ring (Private Key) to stamp a document; anyone in the village can use your public portrait (Public Key) to verify the seal belongs to you, without knowing how you crafted the ring.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Security of the Chain
sections.content: Summarize how hashing and ECC bind transactions into an immutable chain. If one piece of data changes, the hash changes, breaking the chain.
sections.example: The 'Lego Tower': Every block is a brick. If you try to swap a brick in the middle, the entire tower above it becomes unstable and alerts everyone that the structure has been tampered with.
